original_blind_answer:
Dear Jo,

I'd like to feature the old pencil sharpener in our art room. Everyone uses it before life drawing, and the handle squeaks so loudly that our teacher can tell when someone is still getting ready. I'd record a pencil sliding in, the handle turning and the drawer rattling as the shavings fall out. After a moment of silence, listeners would hear the first soft strokes on paper. Then I'd give them a second to guess before naming our object.

Yours,
Li Hua

original_blind_answer:
I picked up the roll and called May over. “Put your toe here.” While she held the bottom of the paper level with the floor, I taped its edge beside the marks. We copied each line across with Dad's pencil, adding the dates. May insisted on drawing the crooked red one herself. When Dad called up the stairs, she tucked the roll under her yellow coat and went down without looking back.

That evening, Dad found us in the kitchen of our new flat. May was holding the paper against the cupboard while I hunted for the end of the tape. Dad knelt down to make sure the bottom touched the floor. When he straightened up, May was already standing beside her four-year-old line. “There's room,” she said, tapping the paper above my blue mark. Dad fetched his pencil. This time she pushed him against the wall and made him take his shoes off.
